To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the crystal structures of the deaminase domain of B. subtiliss RibG and yeast rib2, which catalyse the second and third reactions of the riboflavin pathway, respectively, have been determined.
the crystal structure of the deaminase domain of the B. subtiliss RibG was determined and the mechanism of substrate binding and catalysis in the RibG and Rib2 deaminase domains were investigated.

the structure of the deaminase domain of RibG from B. subtilus was solved and that this structure, in combination with the Rib2 structure, provides a basis for understanding the mechanism of substrate specificity in these enzymes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the deaminases involved in riboflavin and RNA/DNA editing pathways.
the molecular basis of the evolution of the RibG and Rib2 deaminase domains.
the evolution of the deaminase domain in RibG and Rib2, and the structural basis of substrate recognition in RibG.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amino-binding hole is a common feature in all the deaminases, irrespective of their substrate specificity, and it is essential for the catalytic activity of these enzymes.
the deaminase domain is an ancient protein fold and the deaminase activity is an ancient biochemical reaction.

the two consecutive amino acids in the PCXXC motif of B. subtiliss RibG are essential for substrate specificity and that the two consecutive backbones in the PCXXCXG motif of yeast Rib2 are essential for ribitol specificity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two consecutive amino groups in the substrate and product are recognized in the same way by the two enzymes.
these enzymes are a family of deaminases, which are specific for the substrate carbonyl group, and that the binding hole is a key feature in substrate recognition.
the deaminase domains of B. subtils RibG and Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rib2 are structurally similar, and the amino-binding hole is conserved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two enzymes have a common ancestor and the evolution of the substrate specificity has occurred through the addition or removal of a few amino acids.
the amino-binding hole, which is present in all deaminase superfamily members, is a common structural motif that is essential for the deamination reaction.
a single active site can be adapted to recognize different amino groups by subtle changes in the protein structure.
